measures.what_it_does: Renews the Mount Vernon Transportation Benefit District's 0.2% sales and use tax for ten more years. The money can only pay for transportation work in the city: street repair and maintenance, road capital projects, and bike and pedestrian improvements. The current tax, approved by voters in 2016, ends in spring 2027 unless renewed.
measures.cost_line: Keeps the existing 0.2% (20 cents on a $100 purchase); Mount Vernon's combined sales tax stays at 9.0%. The city estimates $2.3 million a year.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Mount Vernon Transportation Benefit District Pro Committee, spokesperson LuAnne Gordan Burkhart) says the tax pays only for transportation, visitors share the cost, and the city is simply asking to continue it at the same rate. It credits the tax with matching grants and with work on the College Way/I-5 interchange, the Hoag Road/LaVenture signal, street overlays and 436 crosswalks and curbs.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one. Councilmember Andrew Vander Stoep voted to put it on the ballot but said he would not support the tax, calling sales tax 'a pretty regressive tax.'

taxes.basis: A yes vote renews an existing 0.2% sales tax at the same rate for ten more years (about $2.3 million a year); the combined rate stays at 9.0%. This is a same-rate renewal, not a new tax.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 18 (S1) and VoteWA record 7426 (S2); the city's ballot filing (S3); the city's Transportation Benefit District page and FAQ (S4); Skagit Valley Herald coverage of the council vote and the 10-year project summary (S5, S6); DOR sales tax rates (S7); 2016 election results (S8); a PDC query showing no committee (S9).

measures.what_it_does: Annexes the City of Sedro-Woolley into the Central Skagit Library District, which already runs the city's library under a contract. City residents would pay the library district's property tax directly instead of the city paying the district, and could vote on library district ballot measures starting in 2027.
measures.cost_line: Library district tax of about $0.232 per $1,000 starting in 2028 (about $517,000 from city property). The city says it will cut its own levy by up to $474,115 to offset most of this, for a net increase of about $11 a year on a $519,450 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (spokesperson Millissa Macomber) says annexation simplifies library funding because residents already pay for the library through the city. It says the council has committed to lowering city property taxes, and that a yes vote gives residents a say on future library bonds or levies.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote puts a new library district property tax (about $0.232 per $1,000) on city property. The city's offsetting cut of up to $474,115 is its stated commitment for 2028, not part of a permanent rate, and leaves a net increase of about $11 a year on a $519,450 home. A small net increase, like other annexations into an existing taxing district.

local-control.basis: A yes vote moves library funding from a city-negotiated contract into a separate district that sets its own levy, and gives city residents a vote in that district in exchange. Like the King County Fire District 43 annexation, it formalizes an existing service relationship rather than changing who provides the service.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 19 (S1) and VoteWA record 7427 (S2); Resolution No. 1191-26 (S3); the city's library annexation page (S4); the Central Skagit Library annexation FAQ (S5); Skagit Valley Herald coverage (S6, S7); a PDC query showing no committee (S8). The city and the Herald link annexation to a possible future library levy lid lift; the library's FAQ says the two are unrelated.

measures.what_it_does: Authorizes a four-year capital levy (2027-2030) for La Conner School District to replace and upgrade technology systems and modernize existing buildings. The district's plans include replacing aging computers and iPads, improving classroom audio-visual systems and repairing facilities.
measures.cost_line: About $0.31 per $1,000 of assessed value each year: $350,000 in 2027 rising to $395,000 in 2030, $1.49 million in total. That is about $154 a year on a $500,000 property.
measures.pro_summary: No statement in favor was filed. Board President Susie Deyo has said the district has been conservative about raising taxes but that the levy is necessary. Board members say upgrading technology before it fails is more efficient.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote adds a four-year capital levy of about $0.31 per $1,000 ($1.49 million total). No expiring capital or technology levy is named; the last La Conner technology levy found on the ballot failed in 2016. It is a new line on current bills, but modest and temporary, like the King precedent for Highline's technology levy.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 20 (S1) and VoteWA record 7428 (S2); Resolution No. 26-14 (S3); Skagit Valley Herald coverage of board meetings (S4-S6); February 2016 election results (S7); a PDC query showing no committee (S8).

measures.what_it_does: Raises Skagit County Fire District 5's regular property tax levy to $0.78 per $1,000 for 2027, up from about $0.34. It then allows revenue growth of up to 3% a year for five years, and the 2031 levy becomes the permanent base. The all-volunteer district serves Allen, Bow, Edison, Samish Island and Chuckanut Drive and plans to use the money mainly to replace aging fire apparatus.
measures.cost_line: $0.78 per $1,000 of assessed value in 2027, up from about $0.3363. The district estimates the increase at about $133 a year on a $300,000 home and $222 a year on a $500,000 home.
measures.pro_summary: The statement in favor (Citizens for District 5 Fire Levy, spokesperson Andrea Leebron-Clay) says the volunteer department faces rising engine, equipment, fuel and operating costs that the 1% limit has not kept up with. It says the levy protects the area's fire protection rating and helps homeowners avoid insurance premium spikes.
measures.con_summary: No statement against this measure was filed; nobody contacted the Auditor to write one.

taxes.basis: A yes vote more than doubles the district's regular levy rate (about $0.3363 to $0.78 per $1,000), allows 3% annual revenue growth for five years and makes the 2031 levy the permanent base. That is a large lid lift, like the Spokane Fire District 9 precedent.

measures.sources_note: Sources: Skagit County local voters' pamphlet page 21 (S1) and VoteWA record 7429 (S2); Resolution No. 2026-1 (S3); the district's levy fact sheet (S4); its Reports & Maps and Leadership pages (S5, S6); the PDC record for Citizens for District 5 Fire Levy (S7) and a 2026 PDC query (S8).
